power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

table.title: Love in Everyday Life in Spain: A Thematic Analysis of Everyday Scenarios of Feeling Loved
table.research_questions: This qualitative phase is exploratory and does not test formal hypotheses. Instead, it aims to identify culturally grounded everyday life scenarios in which people in Spain report feeling loved. The findings will be used to generate testable items for a subsequent quantitative phase. Hypotheses related to cultural consensus and endorsement of these scenarios will be specified and preregistered separately for the quantitative study.
table.study_type: Observational Study - Data is collected from study subjects that are not randomly assigned to a treatment. This includes surveys, “natural experiments,” and regression discontinuity designs.
table.blinding: No blinding is involved in this study.
table.study_design_overview:
This is a qualitative, observational, cross-sectional study using a contemporary iterative approach to thematic analysis. Data are drawn from semi-structured interviews and focus groups with Spanish adults. In the initial phase, expert reviewers conducted inductive coding to identify culturally grounded everyday life scenarios in which people in Spain feel loved. In the current preregistered phase, a team of graduate coders will apply a primarily deductive coding scheme to the full transcripts using Atlas.ti, identifying (1) the presence of the expert-generated scenarios and (2) the relational tie involved (e.g., family member, friend, partner, stranger, acquaintance). Coders will also be encouraged to identify new scenarios inductively. Intercoder agreement (ICA) will be assessed at three time points: early, mid, and late in the coding process. Final scenarios will be thematically grouped to inform item development for a culturally grounded Felt Love Questionnaire in the subsequent quantitative phase.

The semi-structured interviews and focus groups followed a consistent protocol, prompting participants to describe specific moments in which they felt loved, and to reflect on how love is expressed and recognized in Spanish culture. Example prompts included:

--When you think of “love,” what comes to mind?
--Think back to a time when you "felt loved."  Can you tell me what that felt like for you?
--Do you think Spanish society has a particular way of expressing love?

table.existing_data: Registration following analysis of the data
table.existing_data_explanation: Prior to this preregistration, expert reviewers (including the PIs) read through the interview and focus group transcripts and inductively identified a set of candidate everyday love scenarios. No formal coding, quantification, or analysis of relational ties was conducted at that stage. The current preregistered phase involves a systematic coding process by graduate research assistants who have not previously analyzed the data. These coders will code the transcripts for both the presence of expert-identified scenarios and associated relational ties, and will also be open to identifying new scenarios. Intercoder agreement will be assessed, and thematic grouping will follow.
table.data_collection_procedures: Participants were Spanish-speaking adults residing in Spain, recruited through purposive sampling to ensure diversity in age, gender, sexual orientation, relationship status, relationship preference, education, and socioeconomic status (income). Recruitment was conducted via community outreach, institutional partnerships, and snowball sampling. A total of 100 participants took part in the study: 54 participated in individual, in-person semi-structured interviews, 4 participated in interviews as a couple, and 42 participated in 12 in-person focus groups (with 3–5 participants per group on average). All sessions were conducted in Spanish, audio recorded with informed consent, and transcribed verbatim. All transcriptions were then translated to English for Qualitative coding. Participants received 30 euros as compensation for their time. Eligibility criteria included being age 18 or older and self-identifying as culturally Spanish or a long-term (more than 10 years) resident of Spain. Data collection for this phase is complete.
table.sample_size: The total sample includes 100 participants. Of these, 54 participated in individual in-person semi-structured interviews, 4 participated as couples in semi-structured interviews (group of 2— romantic couple), and 42 participated in in-person focus groups, distributed across 12 groups with 3–5 participants per group on average. Each participant provided a full transcript (interview or focus group contribution), which was transcribed in Spanish and translated into English for analysis. These 100 individual data units will be analyzed qualitatively in this study.
table.sample_size_rationale:
Our target sample size was guided by both methodological standards for achieving saturation in salience and prior experience conducting focus groups on love using cultural consensus theory (CCT). We aimed to conduct up to 10-12 focus groups, each with 3–5 participants, stratified by age group and gender, for an anticipated total of approximately 50 participants. This structure supports intimate, dynamic group discussions while ensuring representation across key demographic dimensions. In addition, we conducted 54 1:1 individual interviews and 2 group interviews (romantic couple) to deepen the breadth and nuance of perspectives. Our final sample included 100 participants total.
This sample size was selected based on Weller et al. (2018), who emphasize salience-based saturation rather than a fixed number of interviews in cross-cultural consensus work. Our prior research suggests that a sample of this size allows for the emergence of shared beliefs while preserving thematic diversity. Recruitment was facilitated through community referrals and snowball sampling, following guidance from Creswell & Poth (2018) on engaging local networks for diverse qualitative samples.
table.measured_variables:
We will extract two primary types of qualitative variables from the transcripts:

1. Everyday Love Scenarios: Coders will identify the presence or absence of culturally grounded scenarios in which participants describe feeling loved. These scenarios are drawn from an initial expert review but coders will also remain open to additional scenarios that emerge inductively.

2. Relational Tie: For each identified scenario, coders will also code the relational tie involved (e.g., family member, friend, romantic partner, acquaintance, stranger). These will be coded using a predefined categorical scheme developed for the study.

Both variables will be coded using Atlas.ti across the full dataset and used in subsequent thematic grouping and item development for the Felt Love Questionnaire.
table.statistical_tests:
This preregistration describes a qualitative phase of a mixed methods study. No inferential statistical models (e.g., ANOVA, regression) will be used. Instead, we will conduct a thematic analysis using a contemporary iterative approach that combines deductive and inductive coding. Coders will analyze transcripts using Atlas.ti to identify (1) the presence of predefined everyday love scenarios and (2) the associated relational tie (e.g., family, friend, partner, stranger, acquaintance).

We will compute descriptive frequency counts for how often each scenario and relational tie appears in the dataset. We will also assess intercoder agreement (ICA) using percent agreement, calculated at three time points (early, mid, and late in the coding process) to monitor consistency. These results will guide thematic refinement and item selection for the development of the Felt Love Questionnaire in the quantitative phase.
table.exploratory_analyses: We may explore whether certain everyday love scenarios or relational ties are more frequently reported by participants of different age groups, genders, sexual orientations, or regional backgrounds. These analyses will be descriptive and intended to generate hypotheses for future quantitative work or cultural subgroup comparisons in item development.

table.title: Shared Beliefs on Love in Everyday Life in Spain: A Cultural Consensus Theory Approach
table.research_questions:
1. In our representative sample of people living in Spain (N=500) there will be a shared agreement (there will be only a single underlying culture identified in the responses) on what makes people feel loved in daily life.

2. Scenarios describing daily life experiences that are centered on the theme of support in needs and goals will be agreed upon as highly likely to be loving. Specifically, the cultural consensus for these items will be ‘likely’ to make people feel loved, specified by the 95% credible interval of the consensus truth estimate above 50. 

3. Scenarios describing daily life experiences that are centered on the theme of physical expressions of love will be agreed upon as highly likely to be loving. Specifically, the cultural consensus for these items will be ‘likely’ to make people feel loved, specified by the 95% credible interval of the consensus truth estimate above 50.

4. Scenarios describing daily life experiences that relate to family will be agreed upon as highly likely to be loving. Specifically, the cultural consensus for these items will be ‘likely’ to make people feel loved, specified by the 95% credible interval of the consensus truth estimate above 50.

5. Scenarios describing daily life experiences that relate to friends will be agreed upon as highly likely to be loving. Specifically, the cultural consensus for these items will be ‘likely’ to make people feel loved,  specified by the 95% credible interval of the consensus truth estimate above 50.

6. Scenarios that describe experiences of controlling behavior and jealousy will be agreed upon unlikely to be loving. Specifically, the cultural consensus for these items will be ‘unlikely’ to make people feel love, specified by the 95% credible interval of the consensus truth estimate below 50.

table.statistical_tests:
The cultural beliefs and individual differences of the expressions of love in daily life will be derived using the cognitive psychometric models rooted in the Cultural Consensus Theory framework (Batchelder et al., 2018; Oravecz et al., 2014). Models from this framework have been used in previous studies exploring beliefs about love (Oravecz et al., 2016; Heshmati et al., 2019). 

First we will extract eigenvalues (up to the first 10) from the correlation matrix of responses from the participants for each of the Felt Love Questionnaire (FLQ) items. We will plot these to visualize changes in the eigenvalues (see, e.g., Batchelder et al., 2018). This is a general first step done in CCT research. This will help us test our first hypothesis. If there is a single underlying culture, we will see a sharp drop after the first eigenvalue and only smooth change afterwards.

After this, we are going to fit the Continuous Response model (CRM, Anders et al., 2014) to the participants’ responses to the FLQ items. While hypothesis 1 assumes that there will be a single underlying culture behind the FLQ responses, the CRM can accommodate more than one underlying culture (i.e., it can fit multiple culture solutions). That is to say that with this model we can derive different consensus truths for the FLQ items based on cultural ‘membership’ (person-specific), where membership is derived from the FLQ data. The CRM will derive the culturally shared consensus answers for each item in the Felt Love Questionnaire. It will also derive for each participant an estimate for their: 
a. cultural knowledge level
b. response bias shift
c. response bias scale.

Related to hypotheses 7-14, we test how sources of individual-level differences in our DVs ( a)-c)) relate to other person-level measures captured through psychological scales (IVs). These person-level predictors include:
a. attachment style
b. Personality style
c. cultural value related to interpersonal concern and conformity
d. Sex
e. How much they report expressing love in daily life in general.
f. How much they report feeling loved in daily life in general.
g. how much they feel loved from different sources (such as family etc.)

text.text: Using a sequential mixed-method approach guided by Cultural Consensus Theory, we examined shared agreement about daily experiences that evoke feelings of love in the Spanish culture.
In Study 1, we conducted semi-structured interviews (n = 54), two-person interviews (n = 6), and focus groups (3-5 participants; n = 40).
Qualitative analyses found recurring experiences centered on explicit affection, dependable support and care, quality time, and thoughtful actions.
In Study 2, a representative sample of Spaniards (N = 502) evaluated these experiences to assess cultural agreement elicit feelings of love.
Cognitive psychometric analysis revealed strong shared agreement.

Experiences most likely to evoke love involved support and dependability, shared quality time, and explicit expressions of love, particularly within close relationships such as family, partners, and friends.
In contrast, controlling or possessive behaviors from romantic or familial ties were unlikely to elicit love.

These findings advance social psychological theory by demonstrating that everyday love can be understood as a form of shared cultural knowledge, specifically a relational social schema that can be empirically identified through Cultural Consensus Theory.
People use the word love to describe a wide range of experiences, from affection and care to moral connection.
These meanings are deeply shaped by cultural, social, and relational contexts.

Social psychological research has long sought to define love, most often through the lens of romantic or familial relationships (e.g., Aron & Aron, 1997; Berscheid, 1994; Fehr, 1988 Fehr, , 2006 Fehr, , 2019;; Hazan & Shaver, 1987; Sternberg, 1986).

text.text: While such models have advanced understanding of how love maintains strong interpersonal bonds, less is known about how love is recognized and enacted in everyday life across sociocultural contexts.
Research on lay conceptions of love offers an important shift in perspective.
Rather than imposing researcher-defined models, this tradition examines how ordinary people conceptualize love in their own terms.

Prototype research demonstrates that people consistently describe love through relational and moral features (e.g., trust, caring, honesty, and friendship) rather than passion or sexual desire (Fehr, 1988 (Fehr, , 2006 (Fehr, , 2019;; Fehr & Russell, 1991).

text.text: Complementary social psychology perspectives suggest that lay understandings of love are shaped by implicit narratives and social categories that organize different varieties of love (Meyers & Berscheid, 1997; Sternberg, 1998), as well as essentialist beliefs about caring for another's well-being as a core feature of love (Hegi & Bergner, 2010).

text.text: From a social-cognitive perspective, these lay understandings can be viewed as shared schemas or social scripts that guide how people interpret interpersonal behavior within specific relationships (Baldwin, 1992; Holmes, 2000).

text.text: Thus, whether behavior is recognized as loving may depend on the behavior itself, the relational role of the person enacting it, and its cultural meaning.

However, this literature primarily captures how people broadly mentally represent love (i.e., its defining features and categories) rather than how those shared meanings are specifically enacted and recognized in everyday life.
Complementing these conceptual approaches, recent work conceptualizes love as a dynamic, momentary process that unfolds in daily life.

The everyday love perspective views love not as a static trait or enduring bond, but as recurring micro-moments of connection expressed through gestures, words, touch, and mutual responsiveness (Fredrickson, 2013; Oravecz et al., 2020).

text.text: Empirical studies demonstrate that frequent experiences of felt love are associated with greater well-being, lower loneliness, and psychological flourishing (Major et al., 2018; Dickens et al., 2021; Zhou et al., 2022).

text.text: These findings underscore that love is embedded in ordinary exchanges across diverse relational contexts, not only romantic partnerships, but also interactions with family members, friends, colleagues, and even strangers (West et al., 2025; Williams et al., 2025c).

text.text: Yet despite growing recognition that love operates through daily experiences, little research has examined whether the situations that elicit feelings of love are culturally shared within a society.
Culture plays a central role in shaping emotional meaning.
What signifies love in one cultural context may not carry the same significance in another (Karandashev, 2015).
text.formatted: What signifies love in one cultural context may not carry the same significance in another <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">(Karandashev, 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Crosscultural research demonstrates that relational norms, communication styles, and value systems influence how emotions are expressed and interpreted (Markus & Kitayama, 1991; Mesquita & Leu, 2007).
text.formatted: Crosscultural research demonstrates that relational norms, communication styles, and value systems influence how emotions are expressed and interpreted <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">(Markus & Kitayama, 1991;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">Mesquita & Leu, 2007)</ref>.

text.text: For example, collectivistic contexts tend to emphasize responsiveness, obligation, and relational harmony, whereas individualistic contexts prioritize autonomy and personal expression in close relationships (Dion & Dion, 1993).
text.formatted: For example, collectivistic contexts tend to emphasize responsiveness, obligation, and relational harmony, whereas individualistic contexts prioritize autonomy and personal expression in close relationships <ref type="bibr">(Dion & Dion, 1993)</ref>.

text.text: These differences suggest that everyday loving gestures, such as offering practical help, expressing verbal affirmation, or engaging in physical affection, may carry culturally specific meanings as signals of love.
However, most prior research compares predefined constructs across societies rather than identifying culturally grounded understandings from within a single population.
Far less is known about whether members of a given cultural group converge on a coherent, shared model of what makes people feel loved in everyday life.
Cultural Consensus Theory (CCT; Romney et al., 1986) provides a framework for identifying such shared cultural models.
text.formatted: Cultural Consensus Theory (CCT; <ref type="bibr" target="#b63">Romney et al., 1986)</ref> provides a framework for identifying such shared cultural models.

text.text: Rather than assuming universal definitions, CCT conceptualizes culture as a system of shared beliefs and interpretive norms within a group.

Rooted in cognitive anthropology and cognitive psychology, CCT allows researchers to analyze patterns of agreement across individuals, determine whether members of a group converge on a common cultural model, and estimate the degree to which individuals align with that model (Weller, 2007).
text.formatted: Rooted in cognitive anthropology and cognitive psychology, CCT allows researchers to analyze patterns of agreement across individuals, determine whether members of a group converge on a common cultural model, and estimate the degree to which individuals align with that model <ref type="bibr" target="#b73">(Weller, 2007)</ref>.

text.text: Although CCT did not emerge specifically from social psychology, it complements social psychological approaches by providing a formal method for examining shared social knowledge, such as shared relational schemas (Holmes, 2000) about everyday loving behaviors.
text.formatted: Although CCT did not emerge specifically from social psychology, it complements social psychological approaches by providing a formal method for examining shared social knowledge, such as shared relational schemas <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">(Holmes, 2000)</ref> about everyday loving behaviors.

text.text: In domains where no objective "correct" answer exists-such as abstract emotional constructs like love-consensus reflects collectively learned social knowledge rather than factual truth.

Importantly, CCT is traditionally embedded within mixed-method designs and bridges emic and etic approaches: qualitative methods are used to elicit culturally meaningful content, which is then evaluated quantitatively to test for structured consensus (Romney et al., 1986; Weller, 2007).
text.formatted: Importantly, CCT is traditionally embedded within mixed-method designs and bridges emic and etic approaches: qualitative methods are used to elicit culturally meaningful content, which is then evaluated quantitatively to test for structured consensus <ref type="bibr" target="#b63">(Romney et al., 1986;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b73">Weller, 2007)</ref>.

text.text: Contemporary extensions of CCT use formal cognitive and Bayesian psychometric models to estimate the culturally shared model (Batchelder et al., 2018; Oravecz et al., 2015; Weller et al., 2023).

text.text: CCT has been applied to examine everyday experiences of love in the United States using an instrument composed of brief descriptions of everyday experiences known as the Felt Love Questionnaire (FLQ; Heshmati et al., 2019).

text.text: Participants evaluated descriptions of everyday experiences beginning with the prompt "Most people feel loved when…," allowing researchers to model culturally shared beliefs about love-eliciting situations.

Findings revealed strong convergence on small relational gestures-such as receiving compassion or affectionate closeness-as prototypical experiences of feeling loved, indicating the presence of a coherent cultural model.

Subsequent work extended this approach across developmental stages, demonstrating that although specific expressions may shift with age, the underlying cultural structure of everyday love remains detectable (Ellis et al., 2024; Williams et al., 2025c).

text.text: Similar convergence has also been observed among culturally diverse U.S. immigrant samples (Heshmati & Rombaoa, 2025), underscoring CCT's capacity to identify shared emotional meaning systems within heterogeneous populations.

text.text: However, these investigations have been largely confined to North American contexts, leaving open the question of how everyday love is structured in other cultural settings.
Spain provides a compelling context for extending this work.
Spanish society has been described as strongly oriented toward interpersonal bonds, dense social networks, and the centrality of family life (Uskul et al., 2023).

text.text: Rather than reflecting simple "higher collectivism," recent scholarship suggests that Mediterranean cultures are characterized by distinct forms of interdependence and relational dependence that structure social and affective life in specific ways.

text.text: These include normative physical affection (e.g., hugging, kissing, and touch as everyday expressions of care), direct verbal expressions of warmth, and the embedding of love in shared daily routines such as preparing food and spending time together.

Together, this literature positions everyday love not only as a personal feeling or dyadic bond, but as culturally shared relational knowledge (social schema) that structures how people within a culture recognize and enact connection in daily life.

Prior work on lay conceptions of love in everyday life highlights that love is not merely an emotional connection in romantic relationships, but a culturally shaped understanding of what it means to care for, value, and connect with others (Heshmati et al., 2019; Williams et al, 2025b).

text.text: Yet, the majority of this research has been conducted in North American contexts, limiting our knowledge of how everyday experiences of love are structured in societies with different relational and moral beliefs.

The present research addressed this gap through a sequential exploratory mixed-method design conducted in Spain, a culture characterized by communal sociality, expressive emotional norms, and strong family bonds.

Study 1 used qualitative interviews and focus groups to identify naturally occurring situations in which people living in Spain feel loved across different types of relational ties (e.g., family, friends, romantic partner, strangers).
Study 1 used qualitative interviews and focus groups to identify recurring everyday experiences of feeling loved and the relational contexts in which they occurred.
These findings informed development of a culturally grounded set of everyday love experiences for Spain (FLQ-Spain).

These experiences were then evaluated in Study 2, which quantitatively examined the extent of shared agreement among a large representative group of people living in Spain on what makes 'most people' feel loved using a cultural consensus modeling approach.
Together, these studies provide a comprehensive understanding of love as both a lived experience and a collectively held cultural meaning system adopted by people living in Spain.
Understanding everyday experiences of love requires methods that capture cultural nuance and lived meaning beyond quantitative measurement.

text.text: Guided by this perspective, and as the first step of our CCT investigation, we conducted a qualitative study to explore how people living in Spain experience love in their everyday lives and to identify the diverse ways loving experiences showed up in people's lives as they went about their day.
To achieve this goal, we used semi-structured interviews and focus groups with a diverse sample of adults.

text.text: The primary objective of Study 1 was to generate a detailed culturally grounded inventory of everyday love experiences as experienced in Spain.

Specifically, we sought to (a) identify the situations that elicit feelings of being loved, (b) examine the relational ties through which these experiences occur (e.g., family, friends, romantic partners, acquaintances, strangers), and (c) explore the co-occurrences of these experiences across different relational ties.

The findings from this qualitative phase provided the empirical basis for deriving the Spain version of the Felt Love Questionnaire (FLQ-Spain), a set of culturally grounded everyday scenarios used in Study 2 to estimate shared cultural beliefs about love in everyday life in Spain.
This study was preregistered on the Open Science Framework.
This qualitative phase was exploratory and did not test formal hypotheses.
Instead, it aimed to identify culturally grounded everyday life scenarios in which people in Spain report feeling loved.
These experiences provided the empirical inputs for the cultural consensus analyses conducted in Study 2.

The semi-structured interviews and focus groups followed a consistent protocol, prompting participants to describe specific moments in which they felt loved, and to reflect on how love is expressed and recognized in Spanish culture in response to open-ended questions.
Example prompts included: (1) "Think back to a time when you "felt loved."
Can you tell me what that felt like for you?"
(2) "Can you describe a time that you showed love to someone else?"
and (3) "Do you think Spanish society has a particular way of expressing love?"

text.text: ICA was calculated using a partial-overlap method in which partial matches received proportional credit, exact matches received a score of 1.0, and non-overlaps received a 0.

text.text: Given the sequential design, we focus here on the qualitative patterns most central to the development and interpretation of the FLQ-Spain, rather than providing exhaustive coverage of all qualitative results from Study 1.

Specifically, we summarize the most frequent and salient everyday love experiences, the relational ties through which these experiences were described, and how these qualitative findings informed the items for the FLQ-Spain tested in Study 2.

Participants described a wide range of everyday love experiences, most frequently involving physical affection (e.g., hugs and kisses), quality time, care and support during difficult moments, and personalized consideration (e.g., thoughtful gifts, remembering personal details).
Participants frequently described love as it is expressed verbally and through physical affection, particularly hugging, cuddling, and touch.

Verbal expressions most often involved the literal phrase "I love you," especially from parents to children across situations such as daily check-in phone calls, moments of physical affection, and difficult times.
These expressions were also frequently described in romantic relationships, followed by friendships.
Physical gestures were often framed not as intimate or sexual, but as warm, casual, and embedded in daily interactions, such as greetings or expressions of support.
For example, one participant described Spanish expressions of love through the idea of "campechanidad":
For me…a very key word is: "campechanidad."
We are not only close, friendly people.
When we treat each other, when we approach people, when we want to make others feel comfortable and loved with our bodies.
[For example,] "I'm going to play with your hair, oh, how beautiful it is", we cuddle and kiss and hug.

And I think that, in some cultures, publicly, this not only does not happen because it doesn't happen naturally, but it is also often socially punishable.-Non-binary, 27 years old Participants also discussed "kissing on the cheeks," or giving "two kisses," as a culturally familiar form of physical affection.
However, this practice was interpreted in different ways.
Some viewed it as a routine social norm that did not necessarily communicate love, whereas others viewed it as a culturally embedded expression of affection across different kinds of relationships.
Explicit references to kissing romantic partners appeared less frequently.
Thus, physical affection emerged as a salient feature of everyday love in Spain, while also depending on relational and situational context.
Quality Time.
Spending quality time with others was also frequently brought up by participants when describing daily expressions of love.

Participants emphasized that feeling loved often emerged when others expressed a desire to spend time with them, invited them into shared activities, or adapted their own preferences to participate in something meaningful to the other person.
As one participant explained: But I imagine, uh, I don't want to love soccer [fútbol].
text.formatted: As one participant explained: But I imagine, uh, I don't want to love soccer <ref type="bibr">[fútbol]</ref>.

text.text: And he loves that I go with him to watch soccer.

Well, from time to time, I go with him to watch soccer because I know it's something he's looking forward to, even if it's not my favorite thing to do, but sometimes it's something like that to accompany someone who maybe doesn't have another person to accompany him in what he likes.

Well, it makes you feel loved.-Female, 25 years old Participants also described quality time through ordinary social routines or everyday activities, including walking together, watching a movie, shopping, going to the beach, sharing drinks, eating together, or preparing food for others.

Although food was sometimes described as care or nourishment, participants most often emphasized the relational meaning of these activities as opportunities for connection, accompaniment, and shared presence.
Instrumental Support and Care.
Additionally, participants frequently recounted moments in which love was conveyed through offering or receiving support, care and help, especially during difficult times.
These accounts went beyond verbal reassurance and included more active efforts to reduce others' burdens or provide assistance.
Participants often emphasized that support felt especially loving when it was offered without needing to be requested.
For example, one participant described setting aside daily responsibilities to care for their mother during a moment of distress:
There was a moment where she broke down… So my sister and I decided that "today we are going to stop everything."

No studying, no work, nothing… And even though in that moment, my mom didn't want to talk, we just did that for her.-Non-binary, 20 years old Although support and care were most often described within close relationships, participants also recalled meaningful examples involving acquaintances and strangers, such as someone offering a seat, holding a door, paying for something, or helping during a stressful public moment.
Participants discussed giving and receiving gifts more ambivalently than other expressions of love.
Some described material or obligatory gift exchanges as less meaningful, especially when they lacked personal intention.

However, gifts were more likely to be interpreted as loving when they reflected thoughtfulness, effort, or knowledge of the recipient's preferences and needs (e.g., concert ticket to favorite artist, a new kitchen tool to replace a broken one).
Participants also described small, handmade, or food-related gifts as meaningful because they communicated that the giver had remembered and considered them personally.
Personal Details, Attentiveness, and Genuine Interest.
The qualities that made giftgiving feel loving-thoughtfulness and attentiveness to the other person-also appeared repeatedly in other expressions of love.
Participants described feeling loved when others listened carefully, remembered personal details, checked in about important events, or adjusted their behavior in response to the participant's needs.
One participant described listening as a way of communicating care: Listening, letting the person express themselves.
Say a few words of comfort.
I believe that by doing that, you show the person that you care.

There are many times when you don't need to say anything, just listen and let it flow.-Female, 51 years old Participants also often described feeling loved when others remembered details about them, ranging from simple preferences, such as their favorite color, to more deliberate recollections of opinions or needs they had shared previously.
These experiences often appeared alongside other loving actions, such as gift-giving, shared activities, checking in before an exam, or preparing food the person liked.
More broadly, participants described genuine interest in their thoughts, feelings, and well-being as loving because it made them feel considered, included, and personally known.

While the most frequently mentioned experiences centered on physical affection shared time, support, and attentiveness, participants also described a range of less common but culturally meaningful experiences.

These included emotional comfort and reconciliation, guidance and protection, respect for autonomy, spiritual or nature-based experiences, and collective moments of belonging such as being welcomed by a group, cheering together at a sporting event, or singing in harmony.

Although less frequent, these scenarios enriched the conceptual space of the FLQ-Spain by highlighting the frequent and the subtle expressions of love that emerged from participants' lived experiences and narratives.
Participants described loving interactions across diverse relational ties, but most examples involved family, friends, and romantic partners.

Even when the prompts did not specify a particular relational tie, participants drew on examples from these intimate ties, underscoring their centrality in how love is experienced and expressed in daily life in Spain.

Family examples frequently centered on parent-child dynamics across the lifespan, parents expressing affection toward young children through hugs and care to adult children seeking support or life advice with their parents during major life transitions (e.g., first pregnancy, attending university) and difficult times (e.g., breakups, job burnout).

Friendship examples often emphasized companionship (e.g., accompanying to health appointments), shared quality time (e.g., traveling far for a birthday or wedding), emotional support (e.g., joining for a mental health walk), and the significance of non-romantic affection.

Romantic partners were also frequently mentioned, with romantic relationships and passionate scenarios often being the first examples participants raised when describing their general understanding of love.
When prompted about loving experiences with less close relational ties like acquaintances and strangers, participants were able to provide many detailed and valuable examples.
These included welcoming interactions with neighbors, coworkers noticing distress, and strangers offering unexpected help.
For instance, one participant recalled forgetting her bus pass and being unexpectedly comforted by a stranger: And he [the driver] told me no, to get off the bus.
Then, the lady behind me said, "No, don't worry, I'll pay for it."
And she was trying to calm me down all the time because I was nervous and telling her that I was going to pay her back in cash and so on.

But she kept trying to calm me down; she gave me a hug, and she talked to me….-Female, 21 years old Many of the loving accounts were also described without any relational specificity, focusing more on the scenario or behavior itself rather than on who it occurred with.

Participants frequently specified a loving scenario with the focus on the actions-such as Spaniards displaying love through giving other people kisses, offering help, showing affection, or expressing genuine concern-indicating that these examples can be applied in any relationship.
We conducted a co-occurrence analysis to examine how frequently each everyday love scenario appeared alongside different relational ties (see Figure 1).

text.text: Overall, family and romantic partners were the most frequent relational contexts in which participants described feeling loved, followed by friends, with relatively fewer mentions of acquaintances and strangers.
This pattern further highlights the centrality of close relationships in Spaniards' everyday experiences of love.
Distinct patterns also emerged across themes.

Family references most often co-occurred with scenarios involving offering or giving help, support during a hard time, guidance or advice, and caring when sick, reflecting love as dependable care and instrumental support.
Romantic partners were closely linked with unconditional acceptance, spending quality time, and physical affection, underscoring intimacy and mutual responsiveness as hallmarks of romantic love.

Mentions of friends clustered around sharing meals, opening up about personal problems, and insisting on spending time together, suggesting companionship and reciprocity as defining features of friendship love.

Mentions of acquaintances and strangers were rare, but when they occurred, they typically involved small gestures of kindness, such as smiling warmly or offering unexpected help, indicating that even brief encounters can convey a sense of warmth, connection, and love.
Across relational contexts, support during a hard time emerged as the most pervasive expression of love, showing strong co-occurrence with family, friends, and romantic partners.

Together, these findings indicate that in Spain, love is relationally enacted through reliable support, shared time, and embodied care; these are behaviors that anchor emotional connection within everyday life.

text.text: The primary objective of Study 1 was to identify a culturally grounded set of everyday life scenarios through which people in Spain commonly experience feeling loved.

Drawing on the thematic coding, relational-tie analyses, and co-occurrence patterns described above, we developed a comprehensive list of experiences that capture how people in Spain commonly feel loved in daily life.
Identifying culturally meaningful scenarios followed an iterative process.
First, all highfrequency and salient scenarios identified in the qualitative data were compiled and reviewed by the research team.
Scenarios that overlapped conceptually (e.g., help during a difficult time, offering guidance or advice) were merged or refined to avoid redundancy.

Second, we retained several low-frequency but culturally meaningful expressions that participants described vividly (e.g., being warmly welcomed by a new group), as these captured distinctive aspects of Spanish relational life highlighted in interviews.

Third, to maintain comparability with the original U.S. FLQ, select cross-culturally relevant scenarios (e.g., a child snuggles with them) were preserved when they were also mentioned by Spanish participants.

The final set consisted of 61 everyday love experiences organized across six relational contexts (friends, family, romantic partners, strangers, acquaintances, and general/other ties) that together encompass the full range of experiences identified in the qualitative phase.

The results from Study 1 advance the understanding of love as a culturally embedded emotional experience.

Consistent with prototype research demonstrating that laypeople organize love around relational and moral features such as care, trust, and responsiveness (Fehr, 1988 (Fehr, , 2019)), the Spanish narratives illustrate how these features are enacted through culturally patterned practices of presence and accompaniment.

text.text: Because the FLQ-US did not examine love experiences within specific relational ties, whether a similar relational organization would emerge in U.S. samples remains an important direction for future cross-cultural research.

Moreover, when asked what makes Spanish expressions of love distinct from people in Spain, many participants described Spaniards as "affectionate," "touchy," and "passionate," highlighting how physical contact and emotional intensity are socially normative ways of showing care and love.

This resonates with research on familism and relational interdependence in Mediterranean and Latin cultures (Calzada & Brooks, 2013), as well as broader anthropological accounts of high-contact, emotionally expressive societies.

text.text: These findings also position passionate gestures (e.g., hugging, kissing, touching) as everyday expressions of warmth and love across relational contexts, not just limited to romantic settings.

In line with everyday love perspectives that conceptualize love as unfolding through ordinary micro-moments of connection (Fredrickson, 2013; Oravecz et al., 2020), participants located love in daily routines such as sharing meals, coexisting in the same space, and offering help without being asked.

text.text: Such behaviors may similarly communicate that a person is known, valued, and loved.
Importantly, these expressions appear culturally patterned rather than universally generic.

Consistent with scholarship describing Mediterranean societies as structured by dense interpersonal networks and relational interdependence, physical affection, food sharing, and even certain forms of directive care emerge as culturally legible markers of commitment and responsibility across relational contexts (Uskul et al., 2023).

text.text: Together, these patterns suggest that love in Spain is sustained through everyday practices of accompaniment, embodied warmth, and communal engagement within a broader relational ecology.

Having first identified culturally meaningful scenarios of felt love through in-person fieldwork, coding, and co-occurrence analyses, the second step (Study 2) examined the extent to which these experiences reflect shared cultural beliefs about love among Spaniards
Study 2 focused on eliciting layperson judgments about the everyday love experiences identified in Study 1 and their cultural meaning within contemporary Spain.
We asked a large representative sample (N = 502) of people living in Spain to judge these 61 experiences in terms of how likely or unlikely they would make most people living in Spain feel loved.
Our first aim was to determine whether responses reflected a single shared cultural consensus or multiple subcultures in understandings of everyday love.
Our second aim was to characterize which experiences were more or less likely to elicit feelings of love and to examine how these evaluations varied across relational ties.
Following completion of Study 1 and development of the FLQ-Spain, we preregistered six hypotheses (relevant for the current paper) for Study 2 prior to quantitative data collection and analysis.

Specifically, we hypothesized that (1) responses would reflect a single underlying cultural consensus; (2) scenarios involving support for needs and goals would be judged as likely to elicit love; (3) scenarios involving physical expressions of love would be judged as likely to elicit love; (4) family-related scenarios would be judged as likely to elicit love; (5) friend-related scenarios would be judged as likely to elicit love; and (6) scenarios involving controlling behavior and jealousy would be judged as unlikely to elicit love.
For Hypotheses 2-5, "likely" was operationalized as a 95% credible interval for the consensus estimate above 50; for Hypothesis 6, "unlikely" was operationalized as a 95% credible interval below 50.
Details for the preregistration for Study 2 and all the preregistered hypotheses are available in the Supplemental Materials and OSF.

Felt Love Questionnaire-Spain.
The 61-item Felt-Love Questionnaire-Spain (FLQ-Spain) was developed through a comprehensive process of fieldwork and qualitative analysis in Study 1, to ensure cultural grounding in Spanish culture.
This questionnaire consisted of a variety of scenarios that describe concrete situations in which people may feel loved.

text.text: Participants were first prompted with the instructions "We will ask you about your opinion on what most people think of as loving.
As you read about the everyday life scenarios in the next pages, focus not on your own feelings, but on whether you believe these experiences would make MOST PEOPLE feel loved."

Then, participants rated each scenario following the stem 'Most people feel loved when…' on a visual slider from 0 (Unlikely) to 100 (Likely), with the starting point set directly in the middle to reduce survey acquiescence (bias towards the positive).
This was then repeated for all scenarios, yielding a response from each participant for each experience.
Moreover, all 61 scenarios were presented in a random order for each participant in order to reduce ordering effects for item presentation.

The FLQ-Spain scenarios included specific relational ties for most of the scenarios, which could be categorized into: (1) stranger (e.g., "a person they don't know does something unexpectedly nice for them"); ( 2) acquaintance (e.g., "an acquaintance hugs them warmly," "a coworker celebrates their accomplishments"); (3) friend (e.g., "their friend insists on spending time with them"); ( 4) family (e.g., "their parent offers guidance on what is best for them," "their child is happy to spend time with them"); (5) romantic partner (e.g., "their partner wants to know where they are all the time"); (6) general, or non-specified ties (e.g., "someone shows genuine interest in what they think or do," "they cheer together at a sporting event"); and ( 7) other (e.g., "the sun is shining," "they feel one with the universe").

Family-based experiences cluster at the highest end of the scale, followed by romantic partners and friends, with lower endorsement for acquaintances and strangers.

text.text: Hypotheses 2-5 were also supported: the majority of scenarios involving support for needs and goals, physical affection, family, and friends were estimated as likely to elicit love..
At the same time, the model is norm-regulated rather than uniformly permissive.

Consistent with our sixth preregistered hypothesis, controlling and jealous behaviors were generally judged as unlikely to elicit love, whereas some directive or protective behaviors were interpreted as loving when embedded in care, trust, and responsibility.

Notably, romantic-partner scenarios showed greater variability than family-based scenarios, suggesting that the cultural boundaries of autonomy and control may be more negotiated within romantic contexts than within familial ones.

These patterned distinctions demonstrate that love in Spain is not simply equated with warmth or intensity, but is structured by shared moral expectations regarding responsibility, reciprocity, and appropriate involvement.

text.text: Together, the findings indicate that everyday love in Spain is hierarchically organized, normatively bounded, and collectively recognized as a system of relational commitment.

Across two empirical studies, this sequential mixed-method research combined in-person interviews and focus groups with Bayesian psychometric modeling to examine shared understandings of everyday love in Spain.

The exploratory qualitative phase generated 61 culturally grounded experiences that informed the FLQ-Spain and subsequent Study 2 hypotheses, which were preregistered after Study 1 completion and before Study 2 quantitative data collection and analysis.
Cultural Consensus Theory modeling then demonstrated shared agreement across these experiences.
From a social psychological perspective, these findings show how love is recognized through shared meanings by laypeople, relational schemas, and culturally-patterned everyday interactions.
Together, these studies offer an integrated account of love as both lived experience and shared cultural knowledge.
The single-culture consensus indicates that Spaniards share a coherent cultural schema for recognizing how love unfolds in everyday life.
Within this shared cultural model, instrumental support and dependability emerged as central components.
Scenarios describing receiving support during a difficult time, being cared for when sick, and selfless giving reflect a model grounded in reliable care and mutual responsibility.

These experiences were also among the most highly endorsed in prior U.S.-based research (Heshmati et al., 2019), suggesting that reliable care and instrumental support in times of need may represent a broadly shared foundation of felt love rather than a culturally specific feature.

text.text: This suggests that loving experiences function not only as connection, but as core mechanisms of coping and social support.
Everyday supportive behaviors are known to buffer stress and promote resilience (Feeney & Collins, 2015).

text.text: Spending time with others underscored the cultural value placed on shared presence in Spain.
Across relational ties, prioritizing time together was perceived as loving.

This pattern aligns with research linking frequent, high-quality interactions to well-being (Ryff & Singer, 2008) and resonates with Spain's cultural emphasis on convivencia, or living and connecting together in everyday life.

text.text: The strong consensus that explicit verbal affirmations, such as "parents say 'I love you'", are loving, suggests that direct verbal expression occupies a central place in how love is recognized in this cultural context.

Direct verbal expressions complement embodied affection rather than replace it: saying "I love you" functions as an extension of emotional expressiveness, a way to make felt connection visible and reaffirm relational closeness.

Notably, this item was also among the most strongly endorsed expressions of felt love in prior U.S.-based research (Heshmati et al., 2019), suggesting that explicit verbal affirmation may be part of a relational vocabulary shared across cultural contexts rather than a feature unique to this sample.

text.text: At the same time, the consistency with which verbal affirmations were endorsed alongside embodied and presence-based experiences (e.g., spending time together, physical closeness) points to a cultural model in which verbal and nonverbal expressions of love operate together rather than as substitutes for one another (Rojas, 2024).
Within the shared cultural model, family emerged as the strongest and most consistent source of love.
Both qualitative and quantitative results converged on the centrality of parentchild and intergenerational bonds as the primary context for felt love.
Scenarios such as "parents say 'I love you,'" "family supports them in a difficult time," and "child is happy to spend time with them" were highly endorsed.

While the FLQ-US did not have most of its items framed around specific relational ties, comparable family-related experiences (e.g., a child snuggling up to them, spending time with family) also received high endorsement in prior studies (see, e.g., Heshmati et al., 2019; Ellis et al., 2024), suggesting that centrality of family to felt love may not be unique to this sample.

text.text: At the same time, the family-related scenarios with a high consensus in the present study are diverse in experiences, capturing the full range of behaviors through which familism is expressed.
These include verbal expressions of love, receiving support and guidance, providing care, and spending joyful time together.

Notably, family-based directive and involvement behaviors (e.g., a parent insisting on spending time together, wanting to know a child's whereabouts) were also rated as moderately to highly loving (see Figure 4), suggesting that within this cultural model, parental guidance and involvement are themselves read as expressions of care rather than as constraints on autonomy.

text.text: The strong agreement that love is felt when a child willingly spends joyful time with a parent further suggests that parental love in this sample is grounded in mutual affective engagement rather than obligation alone, with love reinforced through shared positive affect rather than duty (Fernández et al., 2005).

text.text: Romantic relationships in Spain appear to be embedded within the same broader cultural model emphasizing security and compassion.
The strongest romantic indicator of feeling loved, "they feel unconditionally accepted by their partner," reflects companionate love rather than romantic intensity alone (Fehr, 1994).
text.formatted: The strongest romantic indicator of feeling loved, "they feel unconditionally accepted by their partner," reflects companionate love rather than romantic intensity alone <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Fehr, 1994)</ref>.

text.text: This suggests that romantic relationships in Spain do not have a distinct cultural script characterized by intensity and romance, but instead align with the same relational principles that structure love in family and friendship contexts.

Consistent with this interpretation, participants strongly agreed that "their partner shows respect for their space or time" makes people feel loved, reinforcing that healthy romantic love is understood as supportive rather than intrusive (Mikulincer & Shaver, 2010).
text.formatted: Consistent with this interpretation, participants strongly agreed that "their partner shows respect for their space or time" makes people feel loved, reinforcing that healthy romantic love is understood as supportive rather than intrusive <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">(Mikulincer & Shaver, 2010)</ref>.

text.text: At the same time, the data reveal a clear cultural boundary between caring involvement and controlling behavior.

Scenarios involving jealousy and surveillance such as "their partner wants to know where they are all the time" and "their partner shows signs of jealousy" were among the least likely to be perceived as loving.

This reaffirms the compassionate nature of love in everyday life for people in Spain as these controlling behaviors are antithetical to the trusting and accepting characteristics of compassionate love (Goetz et al., 2010; Mikulincer & Shaver, 2017; Fehr et al., 2014).
text.formatted: This reaffirms the compassionate nature of love in everyday life for people in Spain as these controlling behaviors are antithetical to the trusting and accepting characteristics of compassionate love <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(Goetz et al., 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">Mikulincer & Shaver, 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">Fehr et al., 2014)</ref>.

text.text: Importantly, not all directive behaviors were evaluated negatively.
Scenarios in which their friend/parent/partner "insists on spending time with them," were generally perceived as loving.
This pattern likely reflects cultural differences in how "insistence" is interpreted in relation to autonomy and relational identity.
Within an interdependent selfconstrual, the self is defined largely through close relationships rather than individual independence (Markus & Kitayama, 1991).
text.formatted: Within an interdependent selfconstrual, the self is defined largely through close relationships rather than individual independence <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">(Markus & Kitayama, 1991)</ref>.

text.text: Accordingly, in the Spanish cultural context, such behaviors may signal a strong desire for closeness and connection rather than an infringement on personal autonomy.

This contrasts somewhat with prior U.S.-based research, where a comparable "insistence" item was rated as more neutral with respect to felt love (Heshmati et al., 2019); given differences in item wording and relational specificity across studies, this contrast should be interpreted with caution, but it is consistent with the possibility that insistence carries different relational meaning across cultural contexts varying in interdependence.
text.formatted: This contrasts somewhat with prior U.S.-based research, where a comparable "insistence" item was rated as more neutral with respect to felt love <ref type="bibr">(Heshmati et al., 2019)</ref>; given differences in item wording and relational specificity across studies, this contrast should be interpreted with caution, but it is consistent with the possibility that insistence carries different relational meaning across cultural contexts varying in interdependence.

text.text: Similarly, the two directive scenarios that were also evaluated as loving, "their partner is protective of them" and "their partner tells them how to live a healthier life," appear to be interpreted as genuine care and investment in a loved one's well-being.

This interpretation aligns with cultural models of familism, in which guidance, protection, and involvement are normative ways of expressing concern and responsibility toward close others (Marin & Marin, 1991).
text.formatted: This interpretation aligns with cultural models of familism, in which guidance, protection, and involvement are normative ways of expressing concern and responsibility toward close others <ref type="bibr">(Marin & Marin, 1991)</ref>.

text.text: The finding that a partner's encouragement toward healthier behavior was perceived as loving diverged from prior U.S.-based findings, where a comparable item was rated as more neutral (Heshmati et al., 2019); however, slight differences in item phrasing across studies limit the inferences we can draw from this comparison.

text.text: The strong consensus on non-romantic, compassionate scenarios and the emphasis on unconditional acceptance in romantic relationships demonstrate that the Spanish love prototype prioritizes security, reliability, and emotional safety over passionate intensity.
This pattern aligns with prototype research identifying acceptance and care as central features of love (Fehr, 1994 (Fehr, , 2006)).
text.formatted: This pattern aligns with prototype research identifying acceptance and care as central features of love <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Fehr, 1994</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Fehr, , 2006))</ref>.

text.text: Beyond close human ties, the consensus results show that Spaniards also locate "felt love" in a small set of nontraditional sources (e.g., pets, nature, etc.).
Consensus on these experiences varied.
The clearest non-human exception was: "their pets are happy to see them"
which received one of the highest consensus estimates across all scenarios, indicating that Spaniards widely recognize affectionate responsiveness from pets as a prototypical loving experience.

This finding aligns with the broader pattern observed throughout the FLQ-Spain, in which love is defined less by abstract meaning and more by moments of mutual orientation, warmth, and responsiveness, core features of positivity resonance (Fredrickson, 2013).
text.formatted: This finding aligns with the broader pattern observed throughout the FLQ-Spain, in which love is defined less by abstract meaning and more by moments of mutual orientation, warmth, and responsiveness, core features of positivity resonance <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(Fredrickson, 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Experiences involving nature occupied an intermediate position.

Feeling close to nature or noticing that "the sun is shining" were viewed as moderately likely to elicit feelings of love, indicating that embodied positive states and environmental comfort can support feelings of warmth and well-being, but are not sufficient on their own to constitute love.

A similar pattern was observed in prior U.S.-based research, where experiential and ambient scenarios, including feeling close to nature, also received relatively lower endorsement compared to interpersonally grounded experiences (Heshmati et al., 2019).
text.formatted: A similar pattern was observed in prior U.S.-based research, where experiential and ambient scenarios, including feeling close to nature, also received relatively lower endorsement compared to interpersonally grounded experiences <ref type="bibr">(Heshmati et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: This cross-context consistency suggests that the interpersonal contingency of felt love may be a feature that extends beyond the Spanish cultural context.

Prior research shows that contact with nature reliably enhances positive affect and connectedness (Capaldi et al., 2014), yet these effects lack the interpersonal contingency that characterizes love as conceptualized in the present framework.
text.formatted: Prior research shows that contact with nature reliably enhances positive affect and connectedness <ref type="bibr">(Capaldi et al., 2014)</ref>, yet these effects lack the interpersonal contingency that characterizes love as conceptualized in the present framework.

text.text: Additionally, the national-anthem scenario was closest to neutral and also showed the largest variability, implying that national symbolism may reliably evoke collective emotion for some, but it does not function as a culturally consensual "love cue" in the same way as care, closeness, and responsive relationship moments (Sullivan, 2018).
text.formatted: Additionally, the national-anthem scenario was closest to neutral and also showed the largest variability, implying that national symbolism may reliably evoke collective emotion for some, but it does not function as a culturally consensual "love cue" in the same way as care, closeness, and responsive relationship moments <ref type="bibr" target="#b70">(Sullivan, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Scenarios referencing shared religious/spiritual belief contexts (e.g., feeling connected to a higher being, feeling one with the universe) showed only moderate endorsement and noticeably higher dispersion.
From a CCT perspective, this pattern suggests that spiritual and religious experiences represent a subcultural rather than population-wide pathway to felt love in Spain.

Spain is characterized by substantial heterogeneity in religious identification and practice-53% of Spaniards declaring themselves as Catholic and only 17% as practicing (Centro de Investigaciones Sociológicas, 2025)-such that spiritual cues may be meaningful for "some people" but are not part of the shared default understanding of what makes "most people" feel loved.
Notably, experiences involving shared belief systems-such as being surrounded by others who share the same religious or spiritual beliefs-did not elicit strong agreement as loving experiences.
This suggests that shared identity or collective meaning, in the absence of direct emotional exchange, is not central to how love is recognized in everyday life in Spain.
Finally, self-directed experiences further clarify this boundary.

Although participants showed relatively high agreement that people feel loved when "they feel love towards themselves," this scenario did not reach the levels observed for relationally responsive experiences.
This pattern suggests that self-love is acknowledged as emotionally meaningful, but is not treated as equivalent to being loved by another.

In line with theories of positivity resonance (Fredrickson 2013 (Fredrickson , 2016)), love in Spain appears to be understood primarily as a relational process, one that is co-created through mutual presence, responsiveness, and care, rather than as a purely intrapersonal state.

text.text: From a social psychological perspective, these findings contribute to understanding love as a socially recognized and relationally situated category of experience.

Love is not merely an individual feeling or internal state, but a relational phenomenon shaped by culturally shared expectations about how care, connection, and responsiveness are enacted in everyday life.

Building on prototype perspectives of love that show that love is primarily composed of key abstract features of care, affection and trust (Fehr, 1988 (Fehr, , 2019;; Fehr & Russell, 1991), the present findings show that love can be recognized through concrete everyday scripts and behaviors involving instrumental support, shared quality time, verbal and physical expressions, genuine interest, and relational role expectations.

text.text: Also, the findings reveal unique patterns of interpersonal relatedness for the culture in Spain, which aligns with social-cognitive perspectives for how certain relationships and interaction patterns can influence people's relational schemas (Holmes, 2000).

text.text: More broadly, this project serves as a proof of concept for integrating culturally grounded qualitative research with quantitative consensus estimation in the study of emotions.

By grounding measurement development in lived experience and then formally testing shared understanding at the population level, this approach bridges a longstanding divide between qualitative and quantitative traditions in emotion and social psychological science.

Applied to love, a construct often treated as either deeply personal or theoretically diffuse, this mixedmethod framework demonstrates how culturally embedded emotional processes can be empirically specified, compared across groups, and studied as shared social phenomena rather than solely private states.
Several limitations of the present research should be acknowledged alongside directions for future work.
First, the qualitative phase was conducted primarily in an urban setting and may not capture regionally specific expressions of love.

Although participants represented diverse ages, socioeconomic backgrounds, and relational experiences, future research should extend qualitative fieldwork to rural and regionally distinct communities.
Importantly, Study 2 tested the resulting scenarios in a nationally representative sample across Spain.
Second, CCT assesses shared cultural knowledge rather than individuals' personal or momentary experiences of love.

Future research could integrate diary or experience-sampling methods to examine how culturally shared love cues translate into lived experiences across time and contexts, and parallel FLQ instruments could test the model cross-culturally.

In addition, cross-cultural comparisons using parallel FLQ instruments could test whether the Spanish cultural model of love, centered on relational responsiveness, warmth, and dependable care, differs from models observed in more individualistic or lower-contact cultural contexts.

Third, although the FLQ-Spain scenarios were developed to capture a wide range of everyday love experiences, the final set necessarily represents a subset of the scenarios articulated during the qualitative phase.

Scenario selection was constrained by conceptual overlap and practical considerations related to questionnaire length and participant burden, which required prioritizing the most salient and broadly interpretable experiences.
As with any experience-based measure, this process may privilege more observable or interactional expressions of love over subtler or context-dependent forms.

Future research could expand or rotate item pools or incorporate complementary elicitation approaches (e.g., narrative vignettes or visual prompts) to further explore how love is recognized in more ambiguous contexts while remaining grounded in culturally shared understandings.
Across two studies, this research demonstrates that love in everyday life in Spain is not merely an individual feeling but a shared cultural understanding of how connection is enacted.
Using qualitative fieldwork and Bayesian Cultural Consensus Theory, we showed that Spaniards converge on a single cultural model of what makes "most people" feel loved.
This shared model is centered on relational responsiveness, dependable care, and shared presence.
Love is most clearly recognized in moments of emotional orientation, supported in times of need, and invited into warm, responsive interaction.

These findings align with conceptualizations of love as a dynamic, co-created process, emerging through micro-moments of mutual care and emotional synchrony (Fredrickson, 2013; Oravecz et al., 2021 , Williams et al., 2025a).
text.formatted: These findings align with conceptualizations of love as a dynamic, co-created process, emerging through micro-moments of mutual care and emotional synchrony <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(Fredrickson, 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">Oravecz et al., 2021</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b78">, Williams et al., 2025a)</ref>.

text.text: At the same time, the findings reveal clear cultural boundaries around what does not count as love.
Symbolic, identity-based, or meaning-oriented experiences (e.g., national symbolism or spiritual connection) were not widely recognized as loving.
Similarly, controlling or possessive behaviors were largely rejected, highlighting that love in Spain is grounded in respect and trust rather than surveillance or obligation.
By grounding this work outside of the United States, the present research extends a literature on love that has been largely shaped by North American samples and assumptions.

Importantly, the findings reveal substantial convergence with prior U.S.-based research: the core of the Spanish consensus (reliable care, support during difficulty, shared presence, and explicit verbal affirmation) closely mirrors the most highly endorsed experiences of felt love documented in the U.S. (Heshmati et al., 2019).
text.formatted: Importantly, the findings reveal substantial convergence with prior U.S.-based research: the core of the Spanish consensus (reliable care, support during difficulty, shared presence, and explicit verbal affirmation) closely mirrors the most highly endorsed experiences of felt love documented in the U.S. <ref type="bibr">(Heshmati et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: This convergence itself is a meaningful finding, suggesting that certain expressions of felt love are shared between these two cultural contexts.

At the same time, the present research makes a distinct contribution by documenting how this shared core is organized relationally in Spain, differentiated across interpersonal ties, and shaped by cultural norms around involvement, guidance, and interdependence, and by demonstrating that the cultural consensus framework can be successfully extended beyond North American contexts.

More broadly, these findings advance social psychological theory by positioning everyday love not merely as an individual emotion or dyadic relationship property, but as a form of shared cultural knowledge that can be formally identified, mapped, and compared across societies.

Studying love as shared relational meaning requires methods that capture both lived experience and cultural coherence.
CCT provides this framework by testing whether a shared cultural model exists and how strongly specific experiences are embedded within it.

In the present studies, the identification of a one-culture solution provides empirical evidence that everyday experiences of love in Spain are organized around a shared cultural schema, rather than fragmented individual interpretations.
This moves the study of love beyond subjective reports toward a formal assessment of collectively held cultural knowledge.
Methodologically, the use of the Bayesian Continuous Response Model (CRM; Anders et al., 2014) represents a significant advance for research on shared relational schemas.

Unlike traditional consensus approaches, the CRM accommodates continuous judgments, estimates uncertainty around each scenario, and separates shared cultural knowledge from individual-level variability in response tendencies and cultural competence.
This distinction is particularly important for emotional constructs such as love, where personal experiences may vary widely even when underlying cultural beliefs are shared.
The CRM therefore allows researchers to model consensus with greater precision while preserving meaningful individual differences.
